summary.text: A carbohydrate is a sugar, a polysaccharide such as starch, or a derivative of these compounds.
Polysaccharides serve as an energy store, as starch and glycogen do, and as structural components, such as cellulose in plants and chitin in arthropods and fungi.
The sugar ribose is a component of coenzymes such as ATP and the backbone of RNA, and the related deoxyribose is a component of DNA.

Both mainly serve as energy stores

items.explain: Polysaccharides serve as energy stores (starch, glycogen) and as structural components (cellulose in plants).

options.label: Chitin
Starch
Glycogen

items.explain: Chitin is a structural polysaccharide in arthropods and fungi, while starch and glycogen store energy.

items.prompt: What makes a monosaccharide like glucose different from other carbohydrates?

options.label: It contains no oxygen atoms in its structure
It is always a chain of several joined sugars
It cannot be hydrolyzed into smaller carbohydrates

items.explain: Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates because they cannot be hydrolyzed to smaller carbohydrates.

items.explain: Sugars linked to other biological molecules form glycoconjugates, found mostly on the outer cell membrane and important in cell-cell interactions.

items.explain: Lactose is abundant in milk, sucrose is extracted from sugarcane or sugar beets, and fructose occurs in honey and fruits.

paragraphs.heading: Sugars and their relatives
paragraphs.text: A carbohydrate is a sugar, also called a saccharide, a larger chain such as starch, or something made from these. Many simple sugars hold carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms in the ratio 1:2:1, so their basic formula is CH₂O and their full formulas look like Cₙ(H₂O)ₙ. Carbohydrates are one of the main families of biomolecules, alongside amino acids, fats and nucleic acids.

paragraphs.heading: Small, medium and large
paragraphs.text: The simplest carbohydrates are monosaccharides, which cannot be hydrolysed, or split, into smaller carbohydrates. Disaccharides such as sucrose are common, and so are the longer chains, polysaccharides and oligosaccharides, such as starch and cellulose. Saccharides can be sorted by how many units are linked together, their degree of polymerisation.

paragraphs.heading: Fuel, frame and genes
paragraphs.text: Carbohydrates do many jobs in living things. Polysaccharides store energy, as starch and glycogen do, and build structures, as cellulose does in plants and chitin in arthropods and fungi. Ribose, a sugar with five carbons, is part of helper molecules such as ATP and forms the backbone of RNA, while its close relative deoxyribose is part of DNA. Sugars and their relatives also play key roles in the immune system, fertilisation, blood clotting and development.

paragraphs.heading: Sugars stuck to other molecules
paragraphs.text: Sugars can be attached to other biological molecules, forming glycoconjugates. The enzyme-driven process that joins them to proteins and lipids is called glycosylation, and the attached sugar is called a glycan. In mammal cells the most common glycoconjugates sit mainly on the outer cell membrane and in fluids the cell releases. They help cells interact with each other, and the N-linked glycans on a protein can even change what it does, sometimes acting like an on-off switch.

paragraphs.heading: On the plate
paragraphs.text: Carbohydrates are central to nutrition. Starch is plentiful in cereals such as wheat, maize and rice, in potatoes, and in foods made from flour like bread, pizza and pasta. Sugars reach us mostly as table sugar, or sucrose, from sugarcane or sugar beet; as lactose in milk; and as glucose and fructose in honey, many fruits and some vegetables. In food talk, carbohydrate can also mean dietary fibre such as cellulose.

paragraphs.heading: A story that starts with cane
paragraphs.text: The history of carbohydrates is partly the history of sugar cane, first grown in New Guinea and later farmed on a large scale in India, where people learned to make crystal sugar. Their chemistry dates to 1811, when Constantin Kirchhoff found that boiling starch with acid produces glucose. The word carbohydrate was first put forward by the German chemist Carl Schmidt in 1844, and in 1856 Claude Bernard discovered glycogen, the form in which animal livers store carbohydrate.
